title: Golders Green: Four admit arson attack on Jewish ambulances
description: Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London. Hamza Iqbal
body: Four men have pleaded guilty to destroying four Jewish community ambulances in an arson attack causing £1m of damage in north-west London. Hamza Iqbal, 20, Rehan Khan, 19, Judex Atshatshi, and Saif Ali, both aged 18, pleaded guilty at the Old Bailey to a charge of destroying or damaging property being reckless whether life would be endangered.The attack, which took place in the early hours of 23 March, saw four vehicles operated by the charity Hatzola set alight in Golders Green.Prosecutors had said they believed the incident was a targeted attack against the Jewish community.The court heard three of the men set fire to the fully stocked ambulances, while a fourth had waited in a nearby car.After the ambulances were set alight, gas canisters exploded inside the vehicles.As well as destroying each of the £250,000 vehicles, the fire damaged four electrical charging stations and cables costing approximately £5,000 each.Leo Seelig, prosecuting, told the court that the Crown Prosecution Service would be arguing that the four men should be sentenced on the basis that the arson attack was related to terrorism.Mrs Justice Cheema Grubb said she would not rule on the question of terrorism at this stage - with defence counsel arguing that there was no evidence for such a connection.The judge said that the four would be sentenced following the outcome a trial of a fifth man, Subhan Ahmed, who has denied assisting an offender.Iqbal and Khan, of Leyton, Atshatshi, of Dagenham, and Ali, of Walthamstow, were remanded into custody.Run by volunteers, Hatzola has served the north London community of Golders Green, which has a large Jewish population, since 1979. Hatzola, the Hebrew word for save or rescue, is a large non-profit, Jewish-led organisation that provides a free emergency medical response and transportation to hospitals regardless of faith by volunteer medics.

schema.headline: Golders Green: Four admit arson attack on Jewish ambulances

title: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: These two women are among nearly 300 Indians missing
description: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stoppedImage source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, S
body: This Indian pilgrim was about to enter Tibet for her dream tour - then her WhatsApp messages stoppedImage source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Subhrasree Chakraborty in Kathmandu a day before she set out for the pilgrimageByIndia correspondentEarly on Wednesday, Sudipto Bhattacharya received what would be the last messages from his wife.She'd sent a picture of a departure stamp in her passport at 07:57 (02:27 GMT) - immigration at the Nepal border was done.Six minutes later, at 08:03, she wrote: we are waiting to enter China. Then the messages stopped.Subhrasree Chakraborty and the group she was travelling with had been waiting to cross into Tibet for the next stage of their pilgrimage to Mount Kailash, the sacred Himalayan home of Hindu god Shiva that Subhrasree had dreamed of visiting for years.The 43-year-old is now among at least 290 Indians reported missing after deadly flash floods struck along Nepal's border with Tibet. Many of those unaccounted for were on the pilgrimage, which resumed last year after being disrupted by the pandemic and then by tensions between India and China. Thousands of Indians have been making their way to Mount Kailash for years. Subhrasree was travelling without her family, as part of a group of about 30 people. A medical technologist working in critical care at a city hospital, she was used to emergencies. She knew CPR and intensive-care procedures and, according to her husband, was physically fit.But none of that has brought her husband Sudipto Bhattacharya any closer to knowing what happened after that final message."After 08:03am, what happened? We don't know anything," he says.Image source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Chakraborty sent her husband a photograph showing her Nepal immigration clearance before she crossed towards Chinese immigration (blurred from source)Subhrasree had been looking forward to the journey for years.The photographs she sent home from Kathmandu, taken just days before she went missing, capture something of that excitement. In one, she stands in a blue tunic in the ornate courtyard of a temple, smiling gently at the camera. In others, she is dressed in red, posing by the ancient brick-and-carved-wood architecture of Kathmandu valley's historic Durbar Square. She told her husband the countryside was beautiful."She was very excited," says Bhattacharya, a government officer. "This was her dream tour."The journey had begun on Friday 21 August.She took the Mithila Express from Kolkata and reached Raxaul on 22 August. From there she crossed into Birgunj and travelled by bus to Kathmandu, arriving that night. She stayed in Kathmandu for three nights, sightseeing.Then, on the morning of 25 August, the group left Kathmandu by bus for Syabrubesi, a small mountain settlement roughly 122km north of Kathmandu and a gateway to the trekking hub of Langtang region. The journey took almost 12 hours - and was not entirely a smooth one. A landslide blocked their route for about four hours before the army cleared the road. But when Subhrasree spoke to her husband, she told him the skies were clear.There was little to suggest what was coming.Image source, Sudipto BhattacharyaImage caption, Chakraborty told her husband she the pilgrimage was her 'dream trip'"She kept saying the weather was good," he says. "She said it was rather warm, it was raining sometimes."The next morning, 26 August, Subhrasree left her hotel shortly after 07:00.Bhattacharya spoke to her on the phone, and the two continued messaging afterwards. Around an hour later, she told him the Nepal immigration formalities were complete and that the group was waiting to cross into Tibet.After clearing Nepal immigration, pilgrims cross the border on foot to the Chinese immigration facility in Gyirong.Bhattacharya believes his wife may have been inside, or close to, the Chinese immigration building when the disaster struck."I knew there would be connectivity issues on the Tibet side," he says. "So I waited for the next message."At about 15:00, he saw reports of the floods in the media. He started calling pilgrims in her group. Nobody answered.He tried the tour operator and then the two managers accompanying the group. Again, there was no answer.The family has heard nothing from Subhrasree since."Have they been rescued? Was this group among those rescued in China?" Bhattacharya asks. "We want to know more."He believes his wife and the others may already have crossed into Chinese territory before the floods struck. But he has received no confirmation of who made it across - or what happened to them afterwards."Please get me a list from the Chinese government," he says. "Missing, dead and rescued. We need an update."Then comes the admission that captures the agony of those waiting at home: "What do I tell you? Sleepless nights, working on the phone."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, The death toll has risen to 475, more than 48 hours after flash floods devastated the Himalayan border regionFor the family of 54-year-old Rina Banerjee, there is more uncertainty.They do not even know which side of the border she was on when they lost contact.Rina, an unmarried private tutor from Kolkata, was travelling alone with a tour operator as part of the same pilgrimage group.Until then, her journey had appeared to be going smoothly. Her nephew, Dwaipayan Mukherjee, says the family had spoken to her over video calls while she was in Kathmandu."She was happy," he says. "She was doing a trip after a long time."Rina was no stranger to mountains. She had travelled in the hills before and gone hiking with her family."She was quite fit," Mukherjee says. "We have gone hiking. We are used to going to the mountains."She had told him about the landslide they encountered on the way the previous day. The group was stuck for about four hours, she had said. The next morning, the tour operator sent a group photograph, which showed Rina  outside the Nepal immigration centre.Like Subhrasree, she had received her departure stamp, Mukherjee says. After that, silence.Image source, Dwaipayan MukherjeeImage caption, Rina Banerjee, a private tutor, had travelled widely in the hills and was an experienced trekker"I don't know whether they crossed the border or not," Mukherjee says.  "Whether they were on the Chinese side or the Nepal side, we are still wondering."For Subhrasree, the two-week tour was to be her first pilgrimage, and a dream she had nurtured for years. Rina, too, had long wanted to make the journey and was no stranger to the mountains.Both women shared what Bhattacharya calls a "wanderlust" - a love of travelling, discovering new places and, in their case, heading into the mountains. Both had joined a group for the pilgrimage of a lifetime. Both appear to have cleared Nepal immigration, and both were believed to have crossed the border.Their names now appear on the Nepal government's official list , externalof 537 missing people. But that offers little clarity - their families still have no idea where they are or whether they are safe. The Kolkata-based tour operator says they have no information about the fate of the group yet.For both families, the journey has ended with the same unanswered question: did the women make it across the border?

schema.headline: Nepal-Tibet flash floods: These two women are among nearly 300 Indians missing

title: NHS bosses warn of chaos in ADHD and autism care
description: Autism and ADHD care is at risk of descending into chaos, NHS bosses are warning, as costs spiral out of control and unregulated private providers cap
body: Autism and ADHD care is at risk of descending into chaos, NHS bosses are warning, as costs spiral out of control and unregulated private providers capitalise on the huge demand for help.The NHS Alliance, which represents health managers, says the current system in England represents a "bad deal" for patients and taxpayers alike.It points to big variations in what the NHS is being charged for assessments and care - in one case, a local health board was paying £300 to £3,000 for similar services.The group says there has been a rapid expansion in new providers – both private firms and charities are involved - and NHS managers are struggling to ensure the quality and safety of care being provided.The government said an independent review into services and what is behind the rising demand, including whether there is over-diagnosis of these conditions, would be published soon. It said it would act on the findings of that, promising a “new national approach” for autism, ADHD and mental health.Ahead of that, the NHS Alliance has been gathering information from integrated care boards, which hold the budgets for local services, about the current state of care.It said a particular problem was the huge variation in what was being charged by non-NHS providers.Unlike for routine operations, like hip and knee replacements, where there is a set tariff for different treatments regardless of whether the NHS or private sector carry them out, for autism and ADHD there are only guide prices that do not have to be kept to.Local health bosses have also reported a rapid increase in providers. One board reported working with 48 providers – four times more than in two years previously.This expansion was causing problems with the ability of boards to check the quality and safety of the care and support being provided.Providers who carry out assessments only do not have to be registered with the Care Quality Commission, the regulatory body for health and care.Rebecca Gray of the NHS Alliance said managers were "caught between a rock and a hard place"."They understand the anguish and frustration caused by long delays in the system as people wait for assessments, treatment and support."But in working to meeting demand they face soaring costs that are running out of control."She said the situation was a "bad deal for patients and taxpayers" and there was a risk the whole system would fall into "chaos".But a spokeswoman for the Independent Healthcare Providers Network said private providers were helping the NHS meet the growing demand by bringing "significant capacity and innovation".However, she agreed there needed to be better co-ordination, including a national tariff to ensure consistent prices were paid by the NHS.Mel Merritt, of the National Autistic Society, said it was clear the system was in crisis."Spending is rising on short-term solutions due to years of a lack of long-term investment in improving services."And she added despite the sums being spent people were still facing "unacceptable" delays.

schema.headline: NHS bosses warn of chaos in ADHD and autism care

title: South of France holiday scuppers Ed Davey's blood donation
description: A summer holiday to the south of France scuppered Sir Ed Davey's attempt to give blood to the NHS.The Liberal Democrat leader had been poised to donat
body: A summer holiday to the south of France scuppered Sir Ed Davey's attempt to give blood to the NHS.The Liberal Democrat leader had been poised to donate at the Brixton Donor Centre but, after filling out paperwork, was told he could not go ahead due to his recent trip to the Charente region.The NHS says those returning from certain parts of France between May and November should wait four weeks before donating due to the risk of mosquito-borne viruses.A Liberal Democrat spokesperson said Sir Ed would return to give blood once the 28 days had passed.His visit to the south London centre was part of a campaign to promote blood donations to "beat the winter crisis" in the NHS.NHS Blood Donation says it needs over 140,000 people to donate blood for the first time this year to meet demand. Blood has a shelf life of 35 days, so stocks need constant replenishing. Earlier this year, the NHS warned it faced "a significant shortfall in blood stocks with hot weather, holidays and high demand all significantly impacting supplies".Gerry Gogarth, director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant said: "We urgently need anyone eligible to donate to book an appointment as soon as they can."Anyone wishing to donate blood can sign up on the NHS Blood Donation website,, external external or use the app to register and book an appointment.There are restrictions on who can donate blood including limits on those who have recently travelled to particular areas. In Sir Ed's case, the risk of exposure to ChikV and Dengue virus in parts of France prevented him from donating. The French regions covered by the restriction are Bouches-du-Rhône, Charente, Dordogne, Hautes-Pyrénées, Haute-Garonne, Pyrénées-Orientales, Var, Gard, Hérault, Isere, Alpes-Maritimes, Vaucluse or Corsica.A Lib Dem spokesperson said: "Ed unfortunately could not give blood today due to recent changes to rules regarding blood donations after travelling to certain destinations."Ed went to the Charente region in France on holiday which poses an infection risk due to mosquito prevalence, he will have to wait 28 days after returning home in order to give blood. He'll be back."

schema.headline: South of France holiday scuppers Ed Davey's blood donation

title: 18 deaths from battery fires show hidden danger of UK's e-bike boom
description: Eighteen people have died and nearly 700 have been injured in fires caused by e-bikes and e-scooters, new data shows.Fatalities recorded by fire and r
body: Eighteen people have died and nearly 700 have been injured in fires caused by e-bikes and e-scooters, new data shows.Fatalities recorded by fire and rescue services across the UK from these fires include cases where people became trapped inside burning homes, died while trying to escape from a fire out of a high window, or from inhaling toxic smoke.More than 2,000 fires were started by e-bikes, e-scooters or their batteries between 2019 and 2025, Freedom of Information requests made by BBC Verify show.The number of incidents has risen year-on-year and nearly half the fires started in homes or garages, the data shows.London Fire Brigade Assistant Commissioner Pam Oparaocha told BBC Verify the service is "increasingly concerned by the significant fire risk" some of these vehicles can pose, especially when modified or bought second hand."From our investigations we know many of the fires we've attended have involved second-hand vehicles or the bike has been modified using parts bought online. We urge people to be extremely careful about where they buy their e-bike or e-scooter from," she added.Footage of fires caused by e-bikes and e-scooters show how quickly the vehicles can start smoking and then apparently explode, causing blazes that spread within minutes.An average of 153,000 new e-bikes have been added to the UK's roads each year since 2020, according to cycling industry trade body, the Bicycle Association.The cost of a new e-bike ranges from around £400 to £4,000 in high street retailers such as Halfords or Decathlon, while second-hand vehicles and unregulated e-bike conversion kits can be found on online marketplaces for as little as £150.Any lithium-ion battery sold in the UK for these vehicles must meet safety requirements set out by the government that ensures the batteries can be charged safely, do not overheat and are protected from damage.The government's "Buy Safe, Be Safe" campaign, external states that while millions of people use these vehicles safely every day, the risk of fire can increase if they don't meet safety rules, are damaged, modified or used with an incompatible charger. It also says people should look for UKCA or CE product safety marks when buying an e-bike or e-scooter.The number of fires caused by e-bike and e-scooter batteries has increased dramatically from 32 in 2019 to 605 in 2025, according to the data gathered by BBC Verify.The highest numbers of incidents were recorded by fire and rescue services in urban areas, with 793 recorded in London over the seven year period, 128 in Manchester, 93 in West Yorkshire, 74 in Merseyside and 73 in Avon.Lithium-ion batteries are useful because they store a huge amount of energy in a small space, Dr Simon Jones at the University of Warwick, who led research into the safety of e-bikes and e-scooter batteries for the Office for Product and Safety Standards, told BBC Verify."However, if these batteries are faulty, over-charged or damaged, the stored energy may be released rapidly in the form of flame jets and burning projectiles," he said."If this occurs in the home this is likely to result in a fast spreading fire that can engulf a room in seconds and block escape routes, trapping people inside. These fires also release toxic fumes from the batteries that pose a serious risk to health."Jahmell Campbell, 24, from London, said when his e-scooter caught fire "it was the loudest explosion I'd ever heard".He was at his grandmother's home in Hither Green in March last year when the vehicle burst into flames by the front door."The only way out was through the window, so I jumped straight out," he said.Campbell said he ran to the back of the building, and realised his grandmother was trapped. He made his father throw a blanket down for her to escape."My dad had to throw her out the window and we had to catch her," he said.His grandmother suffered minor injuries after hitting a windowsill on the way down."Somehow we all made it out with our lives intact, which honestly shouldn't have happened," he added.Six fire engines attended to fight the blaze. The flat, where his grandmother had lived for over 20 years, was destroyed.Several coroners have warned about the dangers posed by these batteries and have issued at least five Prevention of Future Deaths reports since 2023, with recommendations to improve public safety.Among those cases was eight-year-old Luke Albiston-O'Donnell from Birkenhead, who died after inhaling toxic fumes from a house fire caused by an e-bike battery on charge in 2024. Following an inquest, coroner Anita Bhardwaj warned: "The general public do not appreciate the life-threatening risks involved with having lithium-ion batteries, from electronic bikes in this case, stored in domestic properties."Mohsin Janjua, a 28-year-old man from Bradford, died in similar circumstances in 2023. Later investigations found a "catastrophic failure" of the battery in an e-bike conversion kit purchased online from China was "more likely than not" responsible for the fire.Other coroners linked fatalities to e-bikes and e-scooters that did not conform to UK safety standards.Steve Garidis from the Bicycle Association said retailers have invested in developing safe and legal e-bikes but this can be "undermined by illegal and unsafe products often sold through online marketplaces to unsuspecting consumers".The Bicycle Association and the Association of Cycle Traders run an "E-Bike Positive" scheme, external to help consumers identify distributors, retailers and manufacturers that have met current safety standards.They have also called on the government to crack down on the sale of unsafe e-bikes through online marketplaces and tackle the demand for cheap e-bikes and scooters driven by the gig economy.A government spokesperson said: "Unsafe e-bike and e-scooter batteries can pose a serious fire risk, which is why we are taking action to protect consumers."This includes strengthening the responsibilities of online marketplaces to better protect consumers, working with local authorities to identify and remove unsafe products from sale, and helping people make informed choices through our 'Buy Safe, Be Safe' campaign."MethodologyBBC Verify sent Freedom of Information requests to all 49 fire and rescue services in the UK, asking for data on fires where the source of ignition was recorded as an e-bike or e-scooter, including associated batteries. Forty-one provided comparable responses. Greater Manchester and West Sussex were unable to provide data on casualties, fatalities, and the number of fires that happened in dwellings.While some fire and rescue services log e-bikes and e-scooters as a distinct category, others provided data by performing a text search for "e-bike", "e-scooter" and similar keywords. While this provides a reasonable estimate of incidents, some reports may not have been picked up in this search if e-bikes or e-scooters were not mentioned directly.In analysing this data, BBC Verify removed any clear incidents of arson, as well as any incidents that related to mobility scooters.

schema.headline: 18 deaths from battery fires show hidden danger of UK's e-bike boom

title: Uganda's King Oyo: World's youngest reigning traditional monarch dies aged 34
description: The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch. Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown i
body: The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch. Oyo was not officially married, but Akiiki said "the continuity of the Crown is assured"."His Majesty leaves behind a Prince as his heir, whose identity will be formally revealed at the appropriate time, in accordance with the traditions and customs of Tooro Kingdom," he explained.When he became king in 1995 a regency, which included the queen mother, was established until Oyo turned 18 when there was an official coronation.The young king was well respected by his people and according to a report in the Daily Monitor newspaper he promoted causes such as youth empowerment, education and climate conservation, as well as HIV/Aids awareness.The country's largest and most influential traditional institution, the Buganda Kingdom, said it mourned with the people of Tooro following the death of their monarch, labelling him a valuable figure to Uganda.Image gallerySkip image galleryImage source, The Denver Post via Getty ImagesImage caption, When he was 10, King Oyo was pictured on a trip to the US with Queen Mother Best Kemigisa (L) and Mayor of the city of Denver Wellington Webb (R). He was there on a humanitarian mission for Aids orphans in Uganda.Slide 1 of 3, 10-year-old King Oyo of the Kingdom of Toro in Africa, second from left, eyes Denver Mayor Wellington Webb, right, during an introductory meeting with the King's mother, Queen Mother Best Kemigisa Olimi, far left; and Denver First Lady Wilma Webb at the Denver City and County building Monday. The King, the youngest monarch in the world, is visiting Denver on a humanitarian mission for AIDS orphans in Uganda, When he was 10, King Oyo was pictured on a trip to the US with Queen Mother Best Kemigisa (L) and Mayor of the city of Denver Wellington Webb (R). He was there on a humanitarian mission for Aids orphans in Uganda.

title: GTA 6 extended look: What we know after Netflix preview
description: Praise for GTA 6's graphics was more or less universal, with characters displaying photorealistic faces and lifelike movements.Fans were also impresse
body: Praise for GTA 6's graphics was more or less universal, with characters displaying photorealistic faces and lifelike movements.Fans were also impressed by the detailed locations on show, which included the interiors of apartments, rooftop bars and sleazy underground clubs.The preview also showcased the various environments of Leonida, the fictional, Florida-inspired US state where GTA 6 is set.Within Leonida, GTA 6 players can explore Vice City, an area inspired by Miami, which appeared in the hit 2002 game named after the city.The range of different body shapes and sizes among background characters - something rarely seen in video games - was also highlighted by many players watching online.Journalist Ryan McCaffrey said GTA 6 "might be the best-looking game I've ever seen".The impressive visual fidelity has been attributed to the amount of time Rockstar has spent working on the game, and its budget, which is thought to be among the most expensive in video game history.And according to reports, GTA 6's map is significantly larger than the playable area in Rockstar's previous games.YouTuber TGG, who says he was invited to Rockstar North's headquarters in Edinburgh to see the game, says the developer told him the map was twice the size of GTA 5's map. The company hasn't confirmed this officially.Rockstar had already stated that GTA 6 will be a "single-player experience" on launch, leaving fans to assume a follow-up to the incredibly successful online element of its previous games would come later.The Netflix preview was dedicated to showing off the story and gameplay, and was not necessarily expected to highlight any new multiplayer features.Although the launch of the game on 19 November is widely expected to be the biggest of all time, the long-term success of GTA 6 will be judged on how well Rockstar converts players to any new online mode.GTA online, which also launched after the release of GTA 5, remains one of the most-played games in the world, and is thought to have generated billions of dollars for Rockstar.The previous game in the series, GTA 5, also broke records when it came out in 2013 and has sold more than 200 million copies since.Two official trailers for the sixth game have almost 500 million combined views on YouTube, and the Netflix "extended look" on Thursday is being marketed as an event by the streaming service.Next month the company is due to appear at an employment tribunal in Scotland to defend itself against claims it illegally sacked a group of ex-employees for trying to form a union.It strongly denies the accusations, and says the workers were fired on the grounds of gross misconduct.Additional reporting by Thomas Fabbri.

schema.headline: GTA 6 extended look: What we know after Netflix preview

title: Serial rapist police officer passed vetting despite warnings
description: Craig Naylor, chief inspector for HM Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland (HMICS), led a review into Police Scotland vetting processes in 2023.He
body: Craig Naylor, chief inspector for HM Inspectorate of Constabulary in Scotland (HMICS), led a review into Police Scotland vetting processes in 2023.He said the vetting landscape in 2009, though not as strict as today, should still have meant Greer's past would preclude entry to the police.He said: "My view is that he should never have got in at that point, and my view is that in the intervening period, I'm surprised that something didn't come up about that."When I've run vetting in the past, he would not have got in."Asked by the BBC if these were missed opportunities to stop Greer joining the police, Naylor answered, "Yes".A Police Scotland spokesperson said: "We have been completely open and transparent around information which can be shared in relation to the ongoing investigation into Alan Greer."During an interview with the BBC on 20 July 2026 we provided answers to questions relating to Alan Greer's offending during the course of his policing career, which spanned almost 17 years."The investigation has not established any information during his career which could have resulted in his criminal behaviour being identified at an earlier stage."The recruitment and vetting process carried out by Strathclyde Police prior to Alan Greer joining in 2009 will form part of an independent and external review by the National Police Chiefs' Council. "Our absolute priority throughout this investigation is to support victims. As work continues to identify and support everyone affected by this case it is imperative that we do not disclose any information which could be detrimental to that support."The BBC has obtained a confidential briefing document about the case, "Operation Submarine", prepared by the investigation's SIO (senior investigating officer). The document is dated 12 June this year, about four weeks before the BBC contacted Police Scotland over its intention to run a story about the case.It is described as a "high level overview" into Greer's "significant serious sexual offending".Point 3 of the document is headlined "Identified Criminality" and details of the 2002 and 2005 investigations are listed. It states: "Within the current vetting regime, he would not have been granted Recruitment Vetting."The document was provided to the Scottish government and the Scottish Police Authority (SPA), the oversight body tasked with holding senior officers to account.Yet during a public board meeting of the SPA on 30 July, a week after the BBC broke the initial story, none of the SPA board put the details of Greer's vetting issue to DCC Alan Spiers, who was there in place of Chief Constable Jo Farrell.Board member Chris Creegan asked DCC Spiers which of Strathclyde's previous vetting arrangements were of "particular relevance to this case and Alan Greer's own history" but did not press for an answer and no details of Greer's vetting record were disclosed.The SPA told the BBC that only the authority's chairman Alistair Hay and chief executive Chris Brown, who were both present at the meeting, received the briefing about Greer's vetting - and that it had not been shared with Creegan. It said operational briefings were not "routinely shared" with board members.A spokesperson for the SPA said: "Three authority members raised a number of initial questions to seek assurance about the approach being taken, the impact on public confidence - and the assertion that significant changes to vetting regulations would mean an individual such as Alan Greer, would not be able to join policing today."An HMICS inquiry in 2023 identified significant gaps in Police Scotland's vetting processes, including a failure to re-vet legacy staff since the forces merged in 2013.Greer was one of about 8,800 police officers and staff who had still not been re-vetted, more than a third of the total workforce.HMICS also reviewed certain vetting categories from a sample of about 10% of total applications (about 5,500 over four years) and found at least 29 cases where the risk posed by applicants had been "incorrectly assessed" by vetting officers.HMICS made 15 recommendations, including an urgent review of all the identified problem cases as well as introducing annual integrity testing for officers and routine re-vetting every 10 years.Eleven of the recommendations, including the review of the problem cases, have been fully discharged, with work ongoing on the rest.HMICS chief inspector Craig Naylor said: "It is a concern...there are still people who are not vetted three years on [from the review]."Following the review and in response to concern over high-profile vetting failures in England including the case of David Carrick, Police Scotland initiated a "historic data wash".It was part of a vetting improvement plan "to identify any intelligence or allegations that needed further investigation".The Anti-Corruption Unit (ACU) led the project, along with the force's vetting unit, and concluded: "No significant matters were uncovered that the force were not already aware of."Police Scotland confirmed the data wash flagged nothing in relation to Greer.Naylor told the BBC this was another missed opportunity to spot him sooner.A police source told the BBC: "So the data wash was useless then? How can they say there were no missed opportunities to spot Greer sooner?"The question is, how many more Alan Greers have they missed?"Police Scotland added: "We have already stated publicly that the vetting landscape in 2026 is markedly different from that in 2009 and, under current arrangements, Alan Greer's application would not have progressed."Production/additional reporting: Kevin Anderson and Carla BasuFor support and information on the issues raised in this article, visit BBC Action Line.

schema.headline: Serial rapist police officer passed vetting despite warnings

title: How I beat my late-night shopping addiction
description: I was spending £700 a month: How I beat my late-night shopping addictionImage source, Ella HewittImage caption, Ella says she would spend her wages "a
body: I was spending £700 a month: How I beat my late-night shopping addictionImage source, Ella HewittImage caption, Ella says she would spend her wages "as soon as they hit my account"ByDaniel ThomasBusiness reporterYou may well have been there. It's late, you're scrolling on your phone and suddenly feel a strong urge to buy something - only to wake up the next day and regret it.But what happens when those impulse buys become a habit rather than a one-off?One global study suggests 7% of adults, external experience shopping addiction, external - an uncontrollable urge to spend despite the financial consequences - and younger women are more susceptible.Ella Hewitt, from Liverpool, says her shopping addiction got so bad in 2021 that she was spending up to £700 a month on fast fashion she couldn't afford and sometimes never even wore."I didn't grow up with much money, so when I got a job I would spend my wages as soon as they hit my account," says the 24-year-old."That dopamine hit kept me shopping and in the world of social media there is just so much encouragement to do that."She says she would often make purchases on TikTok or Instagram when she was "tired" or "bored", lured by the latest trends on her feeds.Image source, Ella HewittImage caption, Ella says she was "horrified" by the amount she was buyingShe was working as an HR assistant in a school at the time and her spending meant she couldn't afford to move out of her family home."Horrified" by how much she was buying, she began using diversionary tactics to control her spending.One was to put anything she felt like buying on a wish list and wait 30 days. "If I still wanted it, I would buy it, but more often than not I'd find the urge had gone," she says.'I'm way more in control'Ella gave herself an imaginary budget of £1,000 each day to spend on imaginary purchases, which "scratched the itch" of shopping without the cost. And she vowed only to buy something if she could afford to "buy it three times"."Overall, I cut my spending by about 60%," says Ella, who now works as an ethical fashion influencer and plans to launch her own clothing brand. "I'm not perfect. There are times when I will buy things because I want it. But I am way more in control."Image source, JUSTIN TALLIS/AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Some people have deleted shopping apps from their phone to make it harder to spendTips to get your spending under controlWait 48 hours or longer before you purchase something. Often the urge will goDelete saved credit card numbers and shopping apps Write a shopping list before you enter a store or visit a site, and stick to itSet a small budget for guilt-free treats, or create an imaginary oneUnsubscribe from retailer newsletters and alerts and unfollow influencersUse up products before buying new ones; accessorise rather than buying brand new outfits. Know your triggers: If you shop when you feel lonely, bored or stressed, try exercise or talking with a friend instead Seek help: Citizens Advice, Stepchange, Christians Against Poverty and National Debtline can all offer advice on money problems.Sources: The United Nations Federal Credit Union, Christians Against Poverty'I would buy anything that was trending'Image source, Disha PatelImage caption, Dish Patel says her spending meant she was "always broke"Dish Patel, 23, from London, says she was spending so much on clothes, food, make-up and skincare as a student that she "maxed out" her £2,500 overdraft and was "always broke". Like Ella, she thinks she was making up for not having much money as a child, but the joy was always short-lived. "The feeling you get when you open your new parcels is always amazing until the dopamine hit dies down and the cycle repeats."Dish, who now works as a financial planner, says she would buy "pretty much anything that was trending" but her biggest vice was scrolling on shopping apps to pass the time.'I didn't want to spend the money twice'Then, she deleted shopping apps like Asos and Pretty Little Thing from her phone and removed ApplePay to make it harder to buy things in a single click.She even started leaving her bank cards at home when she went to work. "I would bring a packed lunch in and I would buy my train ticket on Trainline the night before... This basically put me in a habit of not spending a single thing and pre-planning my day to ensure I don't spend anything."She also vowed that any time she wanted to buy something, she had to put the same amount of money into her savings or investments. "It worked because I didn't want to spend the money twice." Figure caption, What do you spend too much on?Research last year from Vanquis, a challenger bank, found Gen Z shoppers make more impulse purchases than any other age group, external, closely followed by millennials.And some experts say exposure to social media, with its targeted advertising, influencer culture and seamless one-click checkout, is fuelling the trend, external.Money and Mental Health, a charity, also blames the design of online shopping sites for "minimising the friction around spending money". It points to "pop-ups" that put customers under pressure to spend, and the inclusion of alternative payment methods like Buy Now Pay Later.The BBC has contacted Meta, which owns Instagram, TikTok and Asos for comment.Get in touchAre you affected by issues covered in this story?  Share your experiences.

schema.headline: How I beat my late-night shopping addiction

title: Itauma vs Hrgovic: Can fast-tracked 21-year-old Briton make history on Saturday?
description: British heavyweight Moses Itauma pulls out his phone and scrolls through his pictures.He shows a meme featuring former Nigerian president Olusegun Oba
body: British heavyweight Moses Itauma pulls out his phone and scrolls through his pictures.He shows a meme featuring former Nigerian president Olusegun Obasanjo in traditional attire, standing with his hands on his hips and staring deadpan into the camera."This is how an African dad looks at you when you pursue a career that goes against his wishes and you turn out to be successful," a chuckling Itauma reads aloud to BBC Sport. "That is pretty much my dad."Itauma was born in Slovakia to a Nigerian father and a Slovak mother before moving to Kent as a young child. His parents originally wanted him to become a doctor or a lawyer. But once his older brother turned professional and the family recognised Itauma's exceptional natural talent, their stance softened."Don't worry about school. Just focus on your boxing," his mother eventually said.That decision has paid off spectacularly.At 21, Itauma steps into the ring against Filip Hrgovic on Saturday for the vacant IBF title with the chance to become the second-youngest world heavyweight champion in history. "There's a lot of expectations on my shoulders to carry the flag of British boxing. I just have to live up to it," Itauma says.Victory against Croatia's Hrgovic would put Itauma on the path to becoming the next big name in British heavyweight boxing, with Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua inching closer to the end of their storied careers.Fury, with his Netflix documentaries and larger-than-life personality, has always made himself the attraction. Itauma is more like Joshua - guarded and keeping the media at arm's length."What irritates me most is when people think you're public property," he says."What people don't know about me is that I don't actually want to be in the limelight. The way my career is going, I just have no choice."Like Joshua, Itauma often appears uninterested in the theatrics of fight week. When Hrgovic interrupted during Thursday's news conference, Itauma calmly asked host Adam Smith for the next question.There are similarities in their careers, too.Joshua fought Charles Martin for the IBF title in his 16th pro bout, having boxed 34 rounds. Itauma arrives at his first world-title opportunity a fight sooner and with 31 rounds logged.While Joshua had an Olympic gold medal and a deeper amateur background, victory for Itauma would make comparisons unavoidable - eclipsing Joshua to become the fastest British heavyweight to win a world title.Itauma's trainer Ben Davison, who also worked with Joshua and Fury, believes he has the temperament to handle what comes next."Pressure is a privilege," he says."Moses has already had that pressure for such a long time and I just think it's water off a duck's back."Boxing's best young prospects tend to be handled carefully and are given time to learn before dangerous tests arrive.Itauma, however, has been fast-tracked to his world-title shot.Francis Warren - son of Queensberry chief Frank - first noticed him as a teenager, sparring established professionals. Former British heavyweight champion Jeamie 'TKV' Tshikeva was there even earlier."Moses was a big 11 or 12-year-old, around 75 to 80kg, (11st 11lb to 12st 8lb) and sparred an adult of the same weight," TKV says. "He really showed up, put hands on this grown man, and I was shocked."The guy he sparred was around 25. Imagine going home and telling your wife you got beat up by a kid."Itauma's progress has been marked by destructive stoppages over Dillian Whyte and Jermaine Franklin. They may not be world-beaters, but the manner of those wins strengthened belief Itauma was destined for the top.When Oleksandr Usyk vacated the IBF title and Frank Sanchez agreed to step aside, Itauma's fight with Hrgovic was elevated into a world-title contest.Suddenly, the fast track looked, to some, like a shortcut.Hrgovic - even before the IBF belt was on the line - claimed Itauma had been handed "everything on a plate". On social media, there was a similar feeling - perhaps a final eliminator would have been a more natural way to earn his shot.Itauma, though, has little interest in proving himself to the doubters."It's a lose-lose situation for me because if I win, I've done what people expect, and if I lose, it's just like, I wasn't as good as what I thought," he says."I don't find happiness in trying to please other people's expectations."But what happens when his power does not end the fight? What happens when an opponent is still standing in round eight, still dangerous, still coming back?TKV, who has sparred Joshua, Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley, has seen enough behind closed doors to believe Itauma can handle it."Moses works hard even though he hasn't had to face adversity in his fights or training," he says. "I've never seen him slack. He's fast, sharp, a good learner and I rarely see him get hit."I believe he can do the rounds, too. He has the potential to dominate the division for years."There is no doubt within Itauma's camp that he belongs at this level. But all the outside questions over timing, merit and readiness will fade when the first bell sounds.On Saturday, the prodigy has 12 rounds - if he needs them - to write his own chapter in heavyweight history.

schema.headline: Itauma vs Hrgovic: Can fast-tracked 21-year-old Briton make history on Saturday?

title: Amy Dowden says she can achieve anything after Celebrity Hunted
description: Spoiler warning: This story contains details of the winner(s) of Celebrity HuntedStrictly Come Dancing star Amy Dowden has said winning Celebrity Hunt
body: Spoiler warning: This story contains details of the winner(s) of Celebrity HuntedStrictly Come Dancing star Amy Dowden has said winning Celebrity Hunted has helped her believe she can "achieve anything" following her battle with cancer.The 36-year-old professional dancer won the latest series of the Channel 4 challenge show alongside Strictly's Carlos Gu, claiming a joint victory with actor Brian Conley and his daughter, comedian Lucy Conley.The programme sees celebrities go on the run while an elite team of hunters tries to track them down, in aid of Stand Up To Cancer.The joint victory marked the first time in the show's history that two pairs have managed to stay on the run without being caught.It also marked a reunion for Dowden and Brian Conley, who were paired together on the BBC One dance programme in 2017.The nail-biting finale saw the two pairs jumping on an extraction plane from a beach in north Wales, narrowly escaping the hunters.Dowden was just 32 when she was diagnosed with grade three breast cancer in May 2023, after finding a lump in her breast the day before her honeymoon.She said: "Cancer took a lot away from me in the last two years but I truly feel I've got my confidence back and this has given me the belief I can go on to achieve anything."We got on to that plane, I was just like, 'celebrate!' I grabbed the champagne!"The Welsh dancer made a return to the ballroom floor in 2025, and has been candid about her experiences of the disease, including having a mastectomy, chemotherapy and fertility treatment.She was put into an early menopause as a result of the treatment, which she opened up about in her BBC documentary Strictly Amy: Cancer And Me.

schema.headline: Amy Dowden says she can achieve anything after Celebrity Hunted

title: Hundreds of migrants cross Channel in one day after 10-day lull
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An inflatable small boat pictured in April 2026Nearly 500 migrants have arrived in the UK in one day, in the
body:
Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, An inflatable small boat pictured in April 2026Nearly 500 migrants have arrived in the UK in one day, in the first boats to successfully cross the Channel in 10 days.The seven vessels that made the crossing were the first since 17 August when 250 people arrived.Dinghies arrived in British waters until late into the night on Thursday, with 494 people being brought into the Border Security Command compound in Dover, Kent.The total number is down overall this year, according to BBC Verify analysis of government data.
                                
                                                                
                                                                        
                                                                        
                                                                        
                                                                    
                                                                    
                                                                
                                                        
                                    Tap the questions below
                                
                                    
                                        How many people cross the English Channel in small boats?
                                    
                                                Between 1 January and 27 August 2026, a total of 16,391 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.
                                                These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.
                                                Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.
                                                Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.
                                                Boats that arrived in the UK from 28 August 2025 to 27 August 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.
                                                Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier. At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).
                                                When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.
                                                The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.
                                                    
                                    
                                        Who is arriving in the UK on small boats?
                                    
                                                People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.
                                            
                                                                            
                                                                                    
                                                                                    
                                                                                    
                                                                                
                                                                                
                                                                            
                                                                    
                                                In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.
                                                    
                                    
                                        How else do people stay in the UK without permission?
                                    
                                                Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.
                                                There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.
                                                The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.
                                    Some 16,391 migrants have crossed the Channel so far, down 43% on the same time last year, and a 17% drop from the same point in 2024.Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has said she will not be "complacent" about the falling numbers, and that there is "more we must do"."That is why I have boosted enforcement on the French beaches and overseas and introduced new legislation to tackle the pull factors that draw people here through unsafe and illegal routes," she added.Follow BBC Kent on Facebook,, external X, external and on Instagram, external and listen to BBC Radio Kent on Sounds. Send your story ideas to southeasttoday@bbc.co.uk, external or WhatsApp us on 08081 002250.

title: Sheffield artist defends "unfinished" Ronnie O'Sullivan mural
description: A Sheffield street artist has defended his mural of snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan after the design received criticism - saying that the project is
body: A Sheffield street artist has defended his mural of snooker player Ronnie O'Sullivan after the design received criticism - saying that the project is "unfinished".Chris Ashmore was commissioned to produce the artwork featuring seven-time world champion O'Sullivan for the back wall of the Spot On Snooker Club on Langsett Road.Although many residents said they liked the mural, others described it as "zombie-like", "shocking" and O'Sullivan's face as "skeletal".Ashmore said he was surprised by the viral response online, but confirmed that he had only completed two weeks out of the five assigned to the job, and "touch-ups" were still needed.The local artist said part of the problem was that he had been working from a scaffolding platform which obstructed his view, meaning he didn't get the "full perspective"."I usually use a scissor lift, where you can stand back and see things as a whole, but I couldn't use it as the land is too uneven," he explained."When the scaffolding came down, I came away and boom - it's gone viral."I saw people saying it looks like Michael Jackson or a zombie. I've got thick skin, I'll be OK, but it didn't feel fair."

schema.headline: Sheffield artist defends "unfinished" Ronnie O'Sullivan mural

title: Stadium closures for Old Firm after fan disorder
description: The sanctions relate to the scenes in March after Celtic's penalty shootout victory, when supporters threw fireworks and other missiles, police office
body: The sanctions relate to the scenes in March after Celtic's penalty shootout victory, when supporters threw fireworks and other missiles, police officers were injured and a number of arrests were made.Both clubs gave evidence to an independent judicial panel after being charged under the Scottish FA's disciplinary rule 37, which covers unacceptable conduct at matches.An independent review published last month concluded the incident came within a "very small margin" of becoming a violent mass confrontation. The report, led by Mark Blackbourne, identified failings by both clubs and criticised the Scottish FA for not taking a tougher approach to crowd disorder.In the recent past, the SFA and SPFL have handed down fines and, on occasion, reduced ticket allocations for issues such as the use of pyrotechnics, but the severity of this sanction signals a shift in approach.The SFA has not escaped its share of the criticism by the independent review, but the panel's report provided the governing body with the cover it needed to get tougher on an ever-growing problem.And while it comes as no surprise to see the clubs defending their positions, when the dust settles, the SFA will hope that these sanctions will send out a clear message that unacceptable conduct will no longer be tolerated.

schema.headline: Stadium closures for Old Firm after fan disorder
